=== quote.py
quote.py: does the curator's message at a UTC time hold a quote word for word?

    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21:32Z
    python3 -I quote.py "QUOTE" 2026-09-26T10:21        a prefix: every message of his in that minute

The time is a prefix of his message's timestamp, as show.py takes it (a trailing Z is dropped).
For each message of his at that time it prints one verdict:
  EXACT        the quote is a substring of the message as stored
  NORMALISED   a substring once both have every run of whitespace made one space, ends trimmed,
               and the curly apostrophe U+2019 made a straight one (nothing else is changed)
  NO MATCH     neither; it then prints the longest run of the quote's words that the
               message holds word for word (after the same normalising), for a reader to judge
With the match it prints the message's text around it.

=== trail.py
trail.py: the trail of one entry of POSITIONS.md, from the repository's history.

    python3 -I trail.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --short    the commit list only, one line each
    python3 -I trail.py 86 --at REV   the record as commit REV holds it

Prints:
  1. the entry's text at HEAD (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md: STRUCK at the top, with the
     commit that removed it and the reason its history block gives, and the text as it last stood);
  2. its blocks in POSITIONS-history.md at HEAD, each with the commit that wrote it (the oldest
     commit whose history file holds the block's provenance line). A block's own "commit X" names
     the source it cites, not its writer;
  3. every commit that made or changed the entry's text, oldest first, read from each commit's own
     tree (side branches included): hash, UTC author time, subject, what it did, how the link to
     the text before was made (number, line, title: exact; similarity: score printed), how many
     other entries of POSITIONS.md the commit changed, and the reasons on record: the history
     blocks it wrote, the comments above verbatim copies of the text in the old history file, and
     the commit message.
  4. a cross-check: the old history lines that the numbering block names as earlier texts of this
     entry, and whether each is a text of this trail.

What a commit did:
  created          a text new in POSITIONS.md that no removed or earlier text explains
  changed          a text that replaced another of the same commit (link: number, line, title or similarity)
  moved to history the text left POSITIONS.md and stands verbatim in POSITIONS-history.md
  archived         a verbatim copy stored in POSITIONS-history.md by a later commit
  re-created       a text new in POSITIONS.md made from an earlier text (archived or removed)
  restored         a text back in POSITIONS.md verbatim from POSITIONS-history.md
  renumbered       the same text under a new number (2026-10-13: none -> P-n)
  struck           the number left POSITIONS.md (the first event of a struck entry's trail)
=== later.py
later.py: his messages after an entry's creation that may bear on it, though no commit of the
entry followed them (his later word may have gone into a skill or another record instead).

    python3 -I later.py 148                   (or P-148)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --top 25          how many to print (default 15)
    python3 -I later.py 148 --at 36f7db77c --until 2026-10-21T20:54
                                              the entry's text at a commit, and no message after a time

The candidates are his messages in the coordinating sessions (tlib.COORDINATING) from the entry's
creation on (for an entry struck from POSITIONS.md, its last text is read, and the list runs on
past the removal) (the first commit of its trail that made its text), less those that leads.py already
printed near the entry's own commits. Each is scored by the entry's distinctive terms:
  - its title's words, beyond common words (a stop list, and words in more than a tenth of his
    messages), lightly stemmed (possessive and plural off, cut to 7 letters); each weighs its
    rarity in his messages, log(messages / messages holding it);
  - its names in backticks, weight 3 each.
A term in his own words (lines that do not start with ">") counts whole; a term only in the
exchange around his message (the coordinator's message he answered, by the reply chain, its
reply to him, and the lines he quoted) counts half. A message also gains 8 when it falls in the
30 minutes before a commit that changed a file the entry names in backticks (`compiler.md`), other
than the entry's own commits, in lines that hold a title term (3 when the lines hold none): that
is where his word may have gone. Naming the entry's number (P-148, or as dictated, P148) adds 8 in
his words, 2 in the exchange. A message is a candidate when its weight is at least 5 (MIN) and it
holds a term in his own words or falls before such a commit. Printed: rank, weight, time, whether it
is after the entry's last change, the terms (in parentheses when only in the exchange), the commit
it precedes, and its first 300 characters; then how many candidates there were in all.

=== near.py
near.py: the curator's messages in a window before a UTC time, each with the coordinating
session's message that it answered, found along the transcript's reply chain.

    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z            window 60 minutes before the time
    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z 15m        or 2h, 1d
    python3 -I near.py 2026-09-26T10:22:23Z 15m --cut 2000
                                                        cut each printed text at 2000 characters
                                                        (his and the coordinator's), saying so;
                                                        by default every text is printed whole

For each message of his: its time, source (main, s1, queued: see show.py), session, length and
full text. Then the message he answered: the coordinator's turn that his message follows on the
reply chain (tlib.py says how the chain is read), every text of that turn whole, each with its
time and the file and line it was read from (the first copy, when a resumed transcript replays
it). Before it, one line for each turn the chain passed over as not addressed to him (replies to
Stop-hook feedback, to an agent's message or hand-back, to a task notification or check-in, to a
system reminder), and for each text written after he sent his message; a passed-over turn that
answers a notification and ends with an ask to him (a question mark, "The ask", "I recommend",
"your yes", ...) is marked, and the newest such turn printed whole, since he may have answered
it. When he quotes lines ("> ..."), the text on the chain that holds them is named, and printed
whole if it is not the answer. After it, the last lines of the three turns to him further back
on the chain, for a message that answers an older question. A queued message (sent while a turn
ran) starts at its delivery into the turn; texts written after he sent it are not taken. A
message on no chain the index holds (a queued one never delivered) falls back to the time: the
coordinator's last text before it, passing over replies to Stop-hook feedback.

=== hischeck.py
hischeck.py: check the block of his quotes that a scout's or reader's report ends with.

    python3 -I hischeck.py FILE...

Each FILE holds a block headed "## His quotes" (to the next "## " heading or the end), one line
per quote of his:
    HIS 2026-09-26T10:21:32.097Z | Run Fable judgement as well.
(a line may be wrapped in backticks or start with "- "). The time is a prefix of his message's
timestamp, as show.py takes it (a trailing Z dropped); each message of his at that time is tried,
and the quote is checked as quote.py does:
  EXACT        a substring of the message as stored
  NORMALISED   a substring once whitespace is collapsed and U+2019 made a straight apostrophe
  NO MATCH     neither, in every message at that time (quote.py "QUOTE" TIME shows the nearest run)
  NO MESSAGE   no message of his at that time
Lines of the block that start with HIS but do not parse are counted as BAD FORM. Prints, per
file, the counts and every line that is not EXACT or NORMALISED, with its line number; exits 1
when any line fails or a file has no block.

=== homes.py
homes.py: where a status that an entry of POSITIONS.md states may already live.

    python3 -I homes.py 151            (or P-151)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --top 8    candidates per sentence (default 5)
    python3 -I homes.py 151 --at REV   the three files as commit REV holds them

Splits the entry (the working tree's POSITIONS.md; for an entry struck from it, its text as it
last stood, said so at the top) into sentences, and a sentence into its clauses
at the semicolons outside parentheses; a clause keeps the label that opens its sentence, as
"Built:" or "Still to build:". A clause states a status when it, its label or its sentence holds
one of the status words: built, to build, landed, pending, default, waits, standing go, listed for his
review, open, held, parked, owed, taken, stands at, returns after, not moved, and the like.

For each such clause it lists the candidates that may already hold the same point: the numbered
items of review-queue.md's lists (b) and (c), and the lines of PLAN.md (a numbered sub-line also
carries its parent's item number, and its own number as a fork when the parent counts forks).
A candidate is listed when it names the entry or shares a distinctive term with the clause:
  row N, item N (PLAN's), review-queue item N, fork N, way N, batch N, rung X, phase N, ask N,
  decision X, another entry's P-N, a name in backticks (a commit hash too), a dotted finding
  name such as judge-review.1 or A.skeptic.2
Each shared term weighs by its rarity among the candidates (log of the candidates over those
holding it); naming the entry adds 2; content words shared (four letters or more, beyond common
words) add a little, to order near-ties, and are printed apart. Candidates are ranked by that
weight, and each is printed with what it shares, for the scout to confirm or reject.

=== pointers.py
pointers.py: every line of the record that names an entry of POSITIONS.md by its number.

    python3 -I pointers.py 86            (or P-86)
    python3 -I pointers.py 86 --at REV   the files as commit REV holds them

Searches, at the working tree: explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, POSITIONS.md, PLAN.md,
review-queue.md, HELD.md and BOOT.md; explorations/reviews/open-asks-*.md; and every file under
.claude/skills/. The history files (POSITIONS-history.md, FACTS-history.md) are not searched:
trail.py reads the first, and both only record. A line counts when it holds the number as a word:
P-86 matches, as in "P-86's" or "(P-86)", but P-860 and P-186 do not. A line that names a range
holding the number ("P-85 to P-88") is listed too, marked as a range.
Prints path:line and the line (cut at 400 characters around the number; --whole prints it whole),
grouped by file; the entry's own line in POSITIONS.md is marked.

=== comments.py
comments.py: his saved page comments that bear on an entry of POSITIONS.md.

    python3 -I comments.py 66            (or P-66)

He also comments on pages, and those comments are not in the transcripts. They are saved as
explorations/coordinator/positions-audit/evidence/curator-comments-*.md: a section per thread,
headed "## On <what it was anchored to>", with one bullet per comment, "- HH:MM: "words"".
A section counts when its heading, or a comment counts when its own words, either
  - name the entry's number, also as dictated: P-66, P66, PE66, P 66 (not P-660), or
  - quote its title: a quoted run ("..." or curly quotes) of at least three content words, at
    least 60 % of which are words of the entry's bold title (case, possessives and punctuation
    ignored).
A section that counts is printed whole, with its heading; a comment that counts in another
section is printed with that section's heading. Each with its file and line.

# Pavol's positions, decisions and known ground

## The goal

- P-7 **The goal is to finish what the designers intended, measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to bytecode and running fast.** The judge is `Specification/`, the Working Draft of February 2011 as the revival revises it, with the 2012 Types chapter cited beside it (P-25). The language is not redesigned. The specification is a living document that states the revival's changes (P-95). The floor to measure against is a pure-Java microGPT, not yet written (PLAN phase 6).
- P-8 **Where the designers left no word, he decides by the goal, a compiled microGPT running fast, not by type-theoretic purity, and stays true to the spirit of Fortress.** He accepts the language's unfinished corners rather than stall in theory. He has not read the specification, the type papers or the library, and takes the designers to have known more than he does. So a review checks his decisions against their intent, for errors of commission and of omission; its items are decisions in this file. Detail: `reviews/decisions-review/judgement.md`, "In short".
- P-9 **The search is for microGPT's most readable expression.** In his words, "we are searching for the optimal expression of the microGPT algorithm for readability." The two sources are Fortress's mathematical notation and Iverson's APL notation, with Hsu's data design for data-flow algorithms. The flat program in Hsu's style, C4, fell short, so polishing happens in the vocabulary, the operations the model is written in. C4 is the APL program's target form. Its hyperparameters are tuple bindings, the form an APL strand assignment expands to; the semicolon form of those lines is set aside.
- P-10 **The APL side quest is closed: its remaining ground, tacit functions, characters and nested arrays, is not pursued.** Its sub-language expands APL to Fortress code over native arrays, and its APL microGPT program stays in the walk check (P-30).
- P-11 **The 2D notation is a gimmick: no work on it unless he asks.** Fortify's mathematical rendering bakes one view of a computation into the syntax, though the same mathematics can be written many ways. APL's one glyph for each transformation does that better. It is presentation only, off the path, and no argument for Fortress.
- P-12 **The type checker on interpreter programs comes after the switch-over.** He wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs, and sees it as low-hanging fruit. Today it checks only against the compiler's prelude (F-9). It comes once walk also takes the static coercions that the checker inserts (P-59).

# The conversation around the APL side quest's close and rung 4b

## Why this file exists

Two days of work closed the APL ladder, ran the microGPT program through it, found that its calling convention broke under parallelism, rewrote that convention, and produced a characterization of Fortress from the whole gap ledger. The questions Pavol asked along the way were what moved the work, and they carry his reasons in a way the reports do not. This is the record of those questions.

## What Pavol was after, in his own framing

The toy problem of the whole revival is microGPT, Karpathy's 243-line character-level transformer, and the search is for its most readable expression. Fortress was one candidate: a language claiming a mathematical notation that should bring the code close to the higher-level concepts. APL was Pavol's later discovery, "a different specialized syntax for distilling ideas, in Ken Iverson's tradition", and Aaron Hsu's talks on data design for data-flow algorithms he found "invigorating". The APL side quest began on 2026-09-10 as a question asked while other work ran ("since APL's symbols are Unicode and Fortress is extensible, can APL be a DSL in Fortress?"), became a ladder up Kruger's "Learning APL" on 09-11 because Pavol wanted to learn APL and the book was recommended, was redirected on 09-12 from "an interpreter inside an interpreter" to "convert APL syntax into efficient Fortress code over native arrays", and got its target on 09-13 when Pavol brought the microGPT-in-APL program from another session. The ladder, he said later, was "to keep you busy and expand the probe" while he had not yet read the book. What he hoped for from the Hsu-style flat program was a diamond; what came out, to his eye, was "a few lumps of coal", and the hope for the rewrite was to get closer.

## The questions, in order, and what each revealed

**"Was anything running?"** The iOS client showed a stop button with nothing visible in flight, three times over two days. Each time an inventory (agents, Java processes, file timestamps) showed what was true; twice a worker had finished and its notice was lost to a stop. Revealed: the session's state must be checkable from the tree, not from the UI, which is what the handover file and the commit-as-you-go discipline are for.

**"Explain the loose ends in plain English."** Three: early findings never merged into the ledger (merged the same day as rows 266–283), the ledger's fix list stale by a hundred rows (re-derived later), and two APL chapters skipped by decision. Revealed: an item Pavol has to ask about twice is an item that should have been done or explained the first time.

**"This seems like a serious bug in the Fortress library."** It was not. The frame stack that crashed at pool size 4 is ours, built in rung 4 of the ladder as the calling convention for APL's anonymous functions, and Fortress did what its specification says: the elements of a tuple are evaluated in parallel. Revealed: the distinction between the sealed language and our layer above it has to be stated every time a failure is reported, because the reader reads "Fortress" first.

**"What the fuck is going on? Restate the presumptions, then teach me."** The presumptions: the sub-language translates APL into native Fortress; no interpreter inside the interpreter; and, implied, the expansion should be code a Fortress programmer could have written, keeping Fortress's properties including implicit parallelism. Rung 4 had tried the natural translation of `{⍵…}` to `fn (omega) => …` and hit two walls: the interpreter refuses every nested re-declaration of a name (probes u01–u03), and hygiene renames a binder written by one rule so that a reference written by another never meets it (ledger row 204). It built a global frame stack instead, wrote "FORTRESS_THREADS=1 is assumed" in one line, and no rung ever ran at another pool size. Revealed: the workaround broke the third presumption, it should have been flagged to Pavol when made, and the microGPT program never nests a function, so the universal mechanism was bought for the book and paid for by the program.

**"Is the ledger mixing Fortress gaps with how-to-write-a-DSL knowledge? How much of APL is left, and how hard?"** The 87 APL rows were counted: 46 in a new section on syntax extension, 41 in the language sections; by class 21 implementation gaps, 2 library bugs, 20 design limits, 38 positive facts. Three kinds of row live in one file, and only the first feeds the fix list. On APL: six chapters reached 106 of 214 examples; the other 108 are nested arrays (half the book, a second carrier), characters (tedious), Dyalog's environment (not the language), tacit (a rung), small features (less than a rung, two blocked by the shadowing check). Revealed: Pavol's goal was never the whole of APL; the ladder was a method, and the finish line is the program.

**"How did we get into the side quest? Was microGPT always the goal?"** Answered from the transcript's timestamps: curiosity, then the wish to learn APL, then the redirection to native code, then microGPT on day four. Revealed: the out-of-scope halves of the chapters were never a loss, because the ladder's stated purpose was to find where the extension mechanism gives out.

**"Isn't the universal `Any` boxing everything and cutting off static typing? I assumed the DSL would produce a strongly typed version by inference from the literals outward. Is that ludicrous?"** Not ludicrous, misplaced by one level. The expander is syntactic and infers nothing; the host infers after expansion, and does so for everything the direct rules produce. The one place it breaks is a dfn's parameter, which the APL text does not type; the context does (rows under `⍤1`, planes under `⍤2`), and named functions carry their types on the host declaration. The `Any` boxed functions, never numbers, once per row or plane, which is why the cost was 1.12× and not 10×. Also: rank and depth are different axes; rank we handle in the type, depth (nested arrays) is the wall. Revealed: the design of rung 4b, and Pavol's standard for the backend, which is C4's own typed code.

**"Do the rewrite. Refocus on the readable expression of microGPT. The Hsu-flat Fortress looked suboptimal to my eye."** Decisions taken; the design written the same hour. On "better Fortress through the APL route": the route cannot produce Fortress better than the library entries it expands to, so the vocabulary is where any diamond is, and the rewrite makes the vocabulary the whole backend.

**"Doesn't Fortress have Scala's positional or anonymous parameters? That relates to the ⍺⍵ issue."** Searched the whole in-repo specification draft and the parser: no placeholder, no partial application, no sections; `_` exists only as a discard in a binding position. Exactly the ⍺⍵ issue: with a placeholder there would be no name for hygiene to rename, and the frame stack was a hand-built substitute for the missing feature. APL's tacit spelling is the placeholder-free style that does translate, which is why the rewrite uses it. Revealed: Fortress's model is the mathematician's "x ↦ e", not the combinator tradition, and Sun Labs built a great deal and not this.

**"What is a nat-parameterised type? Where do we need it? Where does it come from?"** A size carried in the type, from the library's own `Vector[\T, nat s0\]` and `Matrix[\T, nat s0, nat s1\]`, so that any function accepting a matrix must quantify over sizes. Our arrays are built at run time from the corpus and the weights and do not unify with sized types statically (row 23); the interpreter matches them at dispatch. Revealed the asymmetry in C4's vocabulary: sizes on parameters, none on results.

**"Why are the views objects? Doesn't Fortress have views? How would Swift, Scala, Kotlin, Rust do this? And did you answer the impedance-mismatch question?"** An array in Fortress is a trait with `get` and `put`, so a view is an object implementing it over other storage: the same idiom as a Swift struct conforming to `Collection` or a Rust struct implementing `Index`, and older than both. The library has row slices; ours cost a fifth as much (measured); rank-3 planes it has not. On the mismatch: the term is right, and the walls are the primitives Fortress lacks: nested arrays, the implicit-argument function, and, at the grammar level, right-to-left glyph reading, which the mechanism handled. The frame stack's failure was not a mismatch between the languages but our workaround meeting Fortress's own primitive.

Not ludicrous. Two corrections to the picture first, then the answer to the typing question, then what it implies.

**Rank and depth are different axes.** APL arrays have a rank (how many dimensions) and a depth (whether elements are themselves arrays). Rank we handle in the type, one overload family per rank, and stopping at three was a budget choice, not a wall: rank four would be one more family. Depth is the wall. A nested array's elements have no single native type, so the carrier would have to be an array of boxes with dispatch on every element, which is the crutch you describe and the reason the flat numeric subset is the only part that maps natively. You have that right.

**The `Any` in the base boxes functions, not numbers.** Every number is a native `RR64` in a native array throughout; the direct glyph rules reach typed library entries (`aplMatMul(a: Matrix, b: Matrix)`). What is untyped is the calling convention for dfns: a dfn is `fn (): Any`, `⍵` is `aplOmega(): Any`, and the rank operator returns `Object` because the rank of its result depends on what the cell function returns, which is known only at run time. That boxing happens once per row or plane, never per element, which is why the cost is 1.12× and not 10×. The damage is real but it is where you said: the general route has no static type, so nothing about it can be checked, overloaded or parallelized statically.

**Where the types can come from.** Here is the fact that decides your question: the expander is syntactic. A grammar rule sees tokens and writes a template; it has no types at expansion time and cannot infer any. So "inference along the generation chain" cannot live in the translation layer. It lives in the host, after expansion, exactly as it does for hand-written Fortress: a binding `X = e` takes its type from `e`, and a call picks its overload from the argument types. The chain you describe from the literals outward already works for everything the direct rules produce. It breaks at one place only: a dfn's parameters, because `{⍵÷…}` says nothing about what `⍵` is.

The way through is that the context does say it. Under `⍤1` the cells are rows, so `⍵` is a vector; under `⍤2` planes, so a matrix; under `¨` over a strand of weight matrices, a matrix. A rule that expands a dfn literal in that position can write `fn (omega: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): … => body`, and a named dfn bound at the top level can carry its type on the host binding, which is what C4 writes by hand (`rmsn(x: Array[\RR64,ZZ32\]): …`). Once the cell function is typed, the rank operator's result type follows by overloading on the function's arrow type, which the ledger has already verified works (row 171, C4's four `rows` overloads). Then `Object` disappears, the frame stack disappears, the general route becomes C4's `rows` and can be a parallel loop, and the expansion of the microGPT program is C4's model function for function. That is the strongly typed backend you want, and the microGPT subset needs nothing beyond it: its four dfns are all applied under `⍤1`, its two inline dfns under `¨` over matrices, and none nests.

What it gives up is the universal dfn: nested dfns, dops, a dfn whose argument rank is unknown at the call. Those are exactly the book's examples, not the program's. What it needs verified first, by one probe: whether the interpreter lets a lambda take its parameter types from the declared arrow type of its binding, or whether the types must be written on the lambda itself, which decides how a named dfn is spelled.

**On "better Fortress through the APL route".** The route cannot produce Fortress better than the library entries the rules expand to; the expansion is defined by the target, and we chose C4. What it changes is where the Fortress lives: the model becomes sixteen lines of notation over a vocabulary, and the vocabulary is reviewed as a library, one typed entry per glyph, rather than as a program. If C4 looks suboptimal to you, that vocabulary is the place to say where, and the rewrite is the occasion to fix it, because every entry gets written again.

So the decision in front of you is a rung 4b as you described it: strip the frame stack and the universal mechanism, type the dfns from context, keep only the microGPT subset, and gate it on the same 40 checks at both pool sizes with the cost measured against C4 at pool size 4, where the 1.49 should come down to about 1.1. I have not started anything; say the word and I write the design here and send the probe out.

- DARPA's HPCS did not take Sun into phase three (2006) and the project lived on at Sun Labs until 2012. His reading: they did no work on performance, "mucked around with syntax", and the promise that a sufficiently advanced compiler would later make mathematical types fast was never true; the funding was pulled for good reason.
- The compiled path is only about ten times the interpreter because numerics are boxed (`FRR64`, no `DADD`); "without unboxed doubles and arrays of doubles, what are we even doing here"; this goes on the priority list (2026-09-15).
- The type checker runs only on the compile path; he wants it usable on interpreter programs and considers that low-hanging fruit (2026-09-15; not a ledger row, see FACTS).
- Hsu's critique of language paradigms as accidental complexity; he is "coming around to his point of view".

## Decisions on record

- 2026-09-14: C4 is the APL target form; C2's tuple hyperparameter form is what a strand assignment expands to; the semicolon form is set aside.

# Run C4: the synthesis of rounds two and three

C4 is a merge, not a new design. Phase 2 of the C series (`explorations/reviews/run-c2-vs-run-c3.md`, section H) listed what each of the two working programs should take from the other; C4 is those two lists applied to one tree, under the same check and the same goldens, so that the APL side quest has one target program. The decision and its reasons are in `explorations/microgpt-run-c-handover.md`.

## What was merged from where

| piece | taken from | why |
|---|---|---|
| the data side: `FlatData` with the float parser, the loaders, `loadParams(dir, name, count, total)` and the `Corpus` object (`tokens`, `positions`, `valid`, `size`, `length`, `token`) | C3, unchanged but for the header | the keys line of the step names the keys (`ids`, `tg`, `vm`, `pos`) as methods of one object where C2 spelled them as `gather`, `ravel`, `block` and `valid` over two globals; the loader reads the nine files straight into the flat vector, so the model has no load function |
| hyperparameters as three untyped tuple bindings | C2 | ledger row 152: a top-level tuple of literals binds; C3's fourteen typed lines were a habit (a binding takes its literal's type). This is also the form the APL sub-language expands a strand assignment to (an APL strand is a Fortress tuple, rung 5), which is what settles it for the target; six untyped declarations to a line, semicolon-separated, also bind (`probes/semicolon`, gap row 175) but have no glyph behind them |
| the layout table `matName`, `matShape`, `matCount`, `matOffset`, `nParams`, `view(p, i)` | C2 | `matShape` returns the pair, as Hsu's `SHP` holds pairs; C3's `matRows`/`matCols` is the same table split in two |
| `x DOT x` in `rmsn` and `rmsn_b` | C3 | `+/⍵*2` is the dot product; the generator `SUM[t <- x] t^2` is a loop in disguise |
| `SUM e` in `sm` | C3 | ledger row 102: `SUM v` parses as a prefix reduction; `BIG MAX` does not and stays a generator |
| varargs `flat` | C2 | ledger row 130; C3's nine typed parameters were a habit |

Here is the assessment; the probe that settles the open part is queued behind the check so its runs do not disturb the timings.

**Short answer: no.** In the C4 model the annotations fall into four groups, and only the first two are required by a mechanism.

1. **Required by the api.** Everything the check imports, so the eight exported functions (`matName` through `learningRate`, including `step` and `adam`), must carry the full signature the api file declares. This is the api contract, not inference. Nine of the model's annotations are in this group.
2. **Required for overload dispatch.** The two `^T` declarations exist only to differ in parameter type (a matrix versus a rank-3 array). Same for the vocabulary's operator and view families: the `nat`-generic array types are the mechanism there, not decoration.
3. **Proven droppable.** Return types on functions and methods (ledger row 21), lambda parameter types (row 131; C3 wrote `fn (i, j) =>` for the mask), and top-level variable types (row 152's tuple bindings carry none). That covers `mask`, `corpus`, the two lambdas, and every return type on a non-exported function.
4. **Open, and the interesting one.** `rmsn`, `sm`, `rmsn_b`, `sm_b`, and the local `h` and `u`. Row 164 is a warning sign in the same area: an untyped lambda made the interpreter take the first overload silently. The mutable locals in the driver (`p: … := …`) are a smaller instance of the same question.

Two facts frame the answer. The interpreter dispatches on run-time values, so removing an annotation changes nothing about what runs or how fast. And row 153 shows annotations are not always enforced anyway: a `fill` lambda declared to return `RR64` stores integers. So the annotations that stay are the api contract, the dispatch, and documentation of the line's shape; for group 4 the probe will say which.

The closing rung of the ladder is the microGPT rung itself, and C4 is its target form.

**What "target form" means in practice.** The APL sub-language is a grammar whose rules expand glyphs to host Fortress code. Rungs 1 to 6 built the base (`AplCore`, `AplSyntax`) against the book's chapters. The microGPT rung writes `microgpt_concise.dyalog` inside a Fortress component, in the sub-language, and its expansion has to be C4's Fortress or read as it: `⍤2` over per-head cells expands to `heads`, `rows` and the batched juxtaposition on rank-3 views; `+.×` to the library product; `×⍤0 1` to `diag`; `⌷⍤0 1` to `pick`; `∘.=` to `onehot`; `⊃,/,¨` to `flat`; `v¨⍳9` to the strand of views; `TOKM[b;]` and `LEN[b]∘.>⍳BLK` to the corpus object; `⎕NREAD` to the loader; `∘←` to Adam's returned triple. C4's vocabulary is the runtime the expansions call, so the sub-language adds glyph rules, not array machinery.

# microgpt in APL

`microgpt.apl` is Karpathy's microgpt as arrays: forward pass, hand-derived backward pass, Adam, training loop and sampling, in ~110 lines of APL. It follows the structure of Nydhal's Dyalog port (github.com/Nydhal/microgpt.apl, MIT) but is rewritten for **dzaima/APL**, an open-source interpreter, which lacks the rank operator `⍤`, matrix inner product `+.×`, `A[i;j]` indexing, padding `↑`, and single-line guards. Each gap is filled with the older idiom, and the older idiom is the more readable one for learning.

## Verified

- Forward loss on the first document: `3.36596694758485` = the scalar oracle's `3.3659669475848504` (15 printed digits).
- Five training steps from the seed-42 weights on the oracle's document order: all five losses match the oracle to 15 digits.
- Finite-difference check on the second document (repeated letter, 8 positions): `wte` rows for a repeated letter and for BOS, `wpe` row 7, agree with backprop to 1e-10.
- 1000 steps in ~13 s on one vCPU; last-50 mean loss 2.32; samples at temperature 0.5 look like names.

A differential-test failure found a confounder on the way: with `nsteps.txt = 5`, the learning rate decayed to zero over 5 steps while the oracle's schedule ran over 1000, so steps 1–2 matched and step 3 did not. `nsteps.txt` now holds two numbers: steps to run, schedule length.

## Run

```
# interpreter (Java 21+; the build needs a JDK)
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/dzaima/APL.git && cd APL && ./build && cd ..
# weights and document order from Python, same seed as microgpt.py
python3 export_weights.py
# train + sample   (nsteps.txt: "<steps to run> <schedule length>", e.g. "5 1000" to check against the oracle, "1000 1000" to train)
export LANG=C.UTF-8 LC_ALL=C.UTF-8
java -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -Dstdout.encoding=UTF-8 -jar APL/APL.jar -f microgpt.apl
```

====
# Provenance

Dropped in by Pavol on 2026-09-14 as `apl-hsu-handover.zip`, from a separate Claude session that redesigned the microGPT data layout after Aaron Hsu's "Designing Your Data" (Functional Conf 2025). Everything here is that session's own work except the weights, document list and export script, which are byte-identical to `../dzaima/w/`, `../dzaima/docs.txt` and `../dzaima/export_weights.py` and are not duplicated.

Not committed: the two slide transcriptions of Hsu's talk (`slides/*.md`, `*.yaml`), which are a transcription of copyrighted material. They sit in the gitignored `research/decks/` for this session, like the Oracle decks; the talk is at https://youtu.be/ozlxUmdYsHA.

`microgpt_flat.py` downloads Karpathy's `names.txt` at run time and contains no code of his.

Status per the handover: `microgpt_flat.apl` (dzaima) is verified against the Python oracle to 15 digits over 5 steps; `microgpt_concise.dyalog` is unverified, derived line by line from it.

The build worker goes as soon as the probe reports.

What the design does, in one paragraph. The focused base keeps only what the 25-line program uses, over C4's vocabulary imported unchanged. There is no frame stack, no `Any`, no `Object`: a function appears in APL text only as a name of a typed host declaration, so `rmsn⍤1⊢X` expands to C4's `rows(rmsn, X)` and picks its overload by type. The two inline dfns are written as the Dyalog's own tacit spelling, `X1∘(+.×⍉)¨wq wk wv`, which is closer to the source than the dfn rewrite the ladder's base forced. Keys stay integers, so the conversions disappear. Every operator pattern in the program is one rule to one typed entry: `+.×⍤2⊢` is the batched product, `×⍤0 1⊢` is `diag`, `⌷⍤0 1⊢` is `pick`, `∘.=⍳` is `onehot`, `⊃,/,¨` is `flat`. The expansion of the `step` block is C4's twenty lines, and the gate is the same 40 checks at both pool sizes with the cost expected equal to C4's on the same host.

What it gives up, on purpose: dfn bodies, `⍺ ⍵`, guards, recursion, dops, and every general form. Those stay in the ladder's base as the record of the climb; rungs 1–6 are not touched.

One thing for you to look at when you have a moment, since the vocabulary is now the whole backend: `run-c4/src/FlatArrays.fsi`, 40 declarations. If C4's Fortress looked suboptimal to your eye, that file is where it shows, and the rewrite is the occasion to say what should read differently.
---
Pavol's goal, restated so the design is judged by it: the readable expression of the microGPT algorithm, with Iverson's notation for the data flow and Fortress's mathematical notation for the pieces. The translation cannot produce better Fortress than the entries it expands to, so the diamond, if there is one, is the pair: the 25-line Dyalog program and C4's vocabulary. This base makes the vocabulary the whole backend, one typed entry per glyph pattern, so that polishing the vocabulary polishes the expansion.
